name: Omoplata from Armbar Control
summary: The Omoplata from Armbar Control is a chain shoulder lock where the attacker exploits the opponent's bent-arm armbar defense by swinging a leg over their head to trap and internally rotate the shoulder for the tap.
description: Master the omoplata from armbar control in BJJ. Complete guide covering chain attack mechanics, finishing details, defensive strategies, and training drills.
target_area: Shoulder joint (rotator cuff, capsule, AC joint)
overview:
The omoplata from armbar control is one of the highest-percentage chain submissions in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, exploiting the most common armbar defense: bending the trapped arm. When an attacker has established armbar control and the defender successfully flexes their elbow to prevent hyperextension, the resulting bent-arm configuration creates an ideal entry angle for the omoplata transition. Rather than fighting against the defender's strongest defensive structure, this technique redirects the attack to the shoulder joint, transforming a successful defense into a new submission threat.

The transition hinges on timing and leg dexterity. The attacker must recognize the arm bend, maintain wrist control with one hand, and swing their far leg over the opponent's head to establish the omoplata position. The critical phase occurs during the sit-up, where the attacker must explosively rotate from a supine armbar position to a seated omoplata position while maintaining shoulder entanglement. Once seated with far hip control established, the finishing mechanics involve progressive forward pressure that internally rotates the shoulder beyond its safe range of motion.

What makes this chain particularly dangerous in competition is the binary dilemma it creates. Keeping the arm straight invites the armbar finish; bending the arm opens the omoplata. Skilled practitioners who master both attacks from armbar control force opponents into a lose-lose decision matrix, dramatically increasing overall finishing rates from this position. The technique rewards practitioners who develop sensitivity to their opponent's defensive reactions and can fluidly shift between attack vectors.

injury_risks.recovery_time: 6-12 weeks for minor tears, 3-6 months for major tears

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 4-6 seconds minimum pressure increase
tap_signals: Physical hand tap on opponent or mat
Physical foot tap on opponent or mat
release_protocol: Immediately stop all forward pressure and rotation
Release leg pinch on shoulder by opening knees
Allow opponent to extract arm slowly at their own pace
training_restrictions: Never spike or jerk the shoulder rotation
Never apply competition speed in training
Always allow opponent access to tap
Stop immediately if opponent rolls forward during escape attempt
Never apply full finishing pressure until advanced belt level
Always control the rate of shoulder rotation throughout the finish

variations_and_setups.description: The primary entry where you swing your far leg in an arc over the opponent's head after recognizing the arm bend defense, threading the knee past their ear to establish the omoplata shoulder entanglement.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent bends arm defensively and there is clear space above their head for the leg to pass without obstruction

variations_and_setups.description: Alternative entry where you rotate your hips first and thread your leg behind the opponent's neck rather than swinging over their head, using a scooping motion to establish the omoplata angle from a tighter starting position.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When the opponent's head position blocks the standard leg swing or when they are actively tucking their chin against your thigh

variations_and_setups.description: Advanced variation where you release both hands simultaneously and use the momentum of your explosive leg swing to establish omoplata position before the opponent can retract their arm, relying on speed rather than grip retention.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: Against opponents who grip-fight aggressively and prevent you from maintaining a reliable wrist grip during the transition

attacker.name: Omoplata from Armbar Control Attacker
attacker.description: Learn to attack the omoplata from armbar control position. Step-by-step execution guide with counters, common errors, and progressive training methods.
attacker.overview: Attacking the omoplata from armbar control requires recognizing the precise moment your opponent bends their trapped arm and immediately transitioning your leg position to trap the shoulder. The technical challenge lies in maintaining wrist control throughout the leg-swing phase — releasing the wrist prematurely allows arm extraction and complete position loss. Advanced execution involves a seamless flow from the supine armbar position to an upright seated omoplata, using explosive hip rotation to close the transition window. The finish demands patient, progressive shoulder rotation with far hip control preventing the forward roll escape that serves as the opponent's primary defensive option.
key_principles: Treat the arm bend defense as an opportunity rather than a setback — the omoplata chain makes armbar control more dangerous, not less
Maintain wrist control with your near hand throughout the entire leg-swing transition to prevent arm extraction during the vulnerable phase
Execute the leg swing with speed and commitment — hesitation allows the opponent to posture up and defend both the armbar and omoplata
Hip rotation from supine to seated must be explosive and fully committed, as half-measures leave you in an indefensible position between two attacks
Far hip control is the critical finishing detail — without it, the forward roll escape is available and high percentage against even well-applied omoplatas
Apply finishing pressure gradually and progressively, using body weight and forward lean rather than jerking or spiking the shoulder rotation
setup_requirements: Established armbar control with opponent's arm isolated across your hips and at least one hand controlling their wrist or forearm
Opponent has bent their trapped arm past 90 degrees as an armbar defense, creating the shoulder angle needed for omoplata transition
Your legs are positioned with at least one leg across opponent's chest or face, providing an anchor point for the transition
Sufficient space between your hips and opponent's shoulder to swing your far leg over their head without obstruction
Opponent is not actively stacking or driving forward, which would compress the space needed for the leg transition

execution_steps.description: When the opponent bends their trapped arm past 90 degrees to defend the armbar, immediately identify this as the transition trigger. Feel for strong bicep resistance against your hip bridge and the arm curling inward toward their chest rather than remaining extended.

Transfer wrist control to your near hand only, gripping firmly around the opponent's wrist with your thumb on the inside. Release your far hand to prepare for the leg transition. This single-hand grip is temporary but essential for maintaining arm isolation through the transition.

Open your legs slightly from the tight armbar squeeze position, creating space for your far leg to swing over the opponent's head. Keep your near leg across their chest as an anchor that maintains upper body control and prevents them from sitting up during the transition.

execution_steps.action: Swing far leg over head and shoulder
execution_steps.description: Drive your far leg in a committed arc over the opponent's head, threading your knee past their ear and positioning your hamstring across the back of their neck and trapped shoulder. Your shin should drape across their upper back as the leg completes the full arc and your calf hooks their far shoulder.
execution_steps.timing: 1-2 seconds, executed as one fluid motion

execution_steps.action: Sit up and establish omoplata angle
execution_steps.description: Explosively sit up by posting your free hand on the mat and driving your torso upright, rotating your hips 90 degrees so your body faces the same direction as your opponent. Maintain the leg triangle configuration trapping their shoulder and immediately shift both hands to control their far hip and belt line.

execution_steps.action: Control far hip to block forward roll
execution_steps.description: Grip the opponent's far hip or belt with both hands, pulling them toward you to prevent the forward roll escape. This grip is the single most important control point for the omoplata finish and must be established before applying any shoulder rotation pressure.

With the opponent flattened and hip controlled, lean your torso forward gradually while keeping your legs tight around their trapped shoulder. The finishing pressure comes from your body weight driving their arm into forced internal rotation while your hip acts as the fulcrum against their shoulder capsule. Build pressure over four to six seconds minimum.

common_counters.counter: Forward roll escape before hip control is established
common_counters.your_response: Prioritize far hip control as your first action after sitting up. If the roll has already started, follow them through by maintaining your leg position around their shoulder and scooting your hips to match their movement, converting the roll into a mounted omoplata or sweep position.

common_counters.counter: Posture up and retract arm during transition phase
common_counters.your_response: Tighten your near leg across their chest to prevent posturing and close the leg triangle around their shoulder quickly. If they successfully retract the arm, immediately return to standard armbar control and re-establish grips before attempting the transition again.

common_counters.counter: Stack and drive forward to compress space
common_counters.your_response: Use your posted hand and far leg as frames to prevent being compressed. If stacking is successful, pivot to a triangle attack since their forward drive exposes the neck, or return to armbar control with adjusted hip position.

common_counters.counter: Turn into attacker to relieve shoulder pressure
common_counters.your_response: When the opponent turns into you, their shoulder rotation actually deepens. Maintain your leg position and use your posted hand to frame against their far shoulder, keeping distance while the turn tightens the omoplata angle. Continue progressive pressure from the adjusted position.

common_errors.error: Releasing wrist control too early during leg transition
common_errors.consequence: Opponent extracts their arm completely through the gap created when legs open, resulting in total loss of the submission chain and return to neutral or guard
common_errors.correction: Maintain near-hand wrist grip throughout the entire leg swing, releasing only once your leg is fully across their shoulder and the omoplata entanglement is secured

common_errors.error: Failing to sit up after completing the leg swing
common_errors.consequence: Remaining supine leaves you unable to control the opponent's hip or apply forward finishing pressure, allowing an easy forward roll escape or posture recovery
common_errors.correction: Commit to an explosive sit-up immediately after your leg crosses their shoulder, posting your free hand on the mat and driving your torso upright in one committed motion

common_errors.error: Neglecting far hip control before applying finishing pressure
common_errors.consequence: Opponent forward rolls out of the omoplata with high success rate, ending up in your closed guard or escaping to a standing position
common_errors.correction: Prioritize gripping the far hip or belt as your absolute first action after sitting up, establishing this control point before attempting any shoulder rotation

common_errors.error: Applying shoulder pressure too quickly or with jerking motion
common_errors.consequence: Risk of serious shoulder injury to training partner from acute rotational force, or opponent panic-rolls causing chaotic positional loss
common_errors.correction: Build finishing pressure gradually over four to six seconds using progressive body weight, allowing the opponent time to recognize the position and tap safely

common_errors.error: Leaving legs loose around the trapped shoulder throughout the finish
common_errors.consequence: Opponent postures up through loose leg control, extracts their arm by straightening up, or creates enough space to initiate a successful forward roll
common_errors.correction: Pinch your knees together and keep active leg pressure around the shoulder throughout the entire sequence, treating leg control as a constant requirement

common_errors.error: Telegraphing the transition by opening legs wide before committing to the swing
common_errors.consequence: Opponent recognizes the omoplata setup from the preparatory leg opening and preemptively retracts their arm or postures up to defend both attacks
common_errors.correction: Minimize the opening movement by swinging your leg in one fluid committed motion with minimal preparatory leg separation, eliminating the visual cue

training_progressions.focus: Developing fluid leg-over-head movement from supine armbar position
training_progressions.description: Practice the leg swing motion with a fully cooperative partner, focusing on the arc path, speed, and landing position of the leg across the shoulder. Perform 20 repetitions per side with zero resistance, building muscle memory for the transition movement pattern before adding any defensive reactions.

training_progressions.focus: Connecting armbar defense recognition to omoplata entry
training_progressions.description: Partner alternates randomly between keeping their arm straight and bending it during armbar attempts. When the arm stays straight, finish the armbar. When it bends, transition to the omoplata. Develop the recognition-to-reaction pathway with 25% defensive resistance over 5-minute rounds.

training_progressions.focus: Sit-up, hip control, and progressive pressure application
training_progressions.description: From an established omoplata position, practice the complete finishing sequence against 50% resistance. Emphasize the timing of far hip control, proper body positioning for the finish, and controlled progressive pressure. Partner provides specific defenses (forward roll attempts, posturing) for the attacker to counter.

training_progressions.focus: Full sequence integration under progressive resistance
training_progressions.description: Start from armbar control against escalating resistance (50% building to 80%). Complete the full chain from defensive recognition through omoplata finish with live unpredictable defensive responses. Alternate between partners for 3-minute rounds, gradually increasing intensity over multiple sessions.

flashcards.question: What specific defensive reaction triggers the transition from armbar to omoplata?
flashcards.answer: The trigger is the opponent bending their trapped elbow past 90 degrees to prevent hyperextension. When you feel strong bicep resistance against your hip bridge and the arm begins curling inward toward the opponent's chest, this indicates they have committed to the bend defense. This bent-arm position creates the exact shoulder angle needed to swing your leg over and establish the omoplata entanglement, transforming their successful armbar defense into a new vulnerability.

trap: Yank the arm straight to finish

flashcards.question: What anatomical structure does the omoplata from armbar control primarily attack?
flashcards.answer: The omoplata attacks the shoulder joint complex, specifically targeting the rotator cuff muscles, the glenohumeral capsule, and the acromioclavicular joint. The finishing pressure creates forced internal rotation combined with extension of the shoulder, stressing these structures beyond their normal range of motion. The shoulder capsule and rotator cuff tendons bear the primary load, with the labrum at risk of tearing in extreme or rapid applications.

flashcards.question: Why is maintaining wrist control during the leg swing the most critical technical detail?
flashcards.answer: Wrist control during the leg swing prevents the opponent from retracting their arm through the gap created when you open your legs to transition. Without wrist control, the brief moment when your legs separate to swing over their head creates a window for complete arm extraction, resulting in total loss of the submission chain. Maintaining near-hand wrist grip bridges the gap between armbar control and omoplata control, ensuring continuity throughout the transition.

trap: Frees your hand to push off

flashcards.question: Your opponent begins forward rolling as you sit up for the omoplata — what is your immediate response?
flashcards.answer: Immediately grip their far hip or belt with your inside hand to block the roll before it gains momentum. If they have already initiated rotation, follow them through the roll by maintaining your leg position around their shoulder and scooting your hips to match their movement. As they complete the roll, you can often end up in a mounted omoplata or transition to a sweep, converting their escape attempt into a positional advantage rather than losing the submission entirely.
flashcards.answer_line: Grip far hip to block roll

trap: Let go and chase the roll

flashcards.question: What is the point of no return for the defender in this submission?
flashcards.answer: The point of no return occurs when the attacker has fully sat up, established tight leg control around the shoulder with knees pinched, and secured a firm grip on the defender's far hip preventing the forward roll. At this stage, the forward roll escape is blocked, arm extraction is impossible due to the leg entanglement, and any remaining defensive movement only accelerates the shoulder rotation toward the finish. The defender should recognize this configuration and tap.

flashcards.question: How should you apply finishing pressure safely during training?
flashcards.answer: Apply finishing pressure gradually over a minimum of four to six seconds by slowly leaning your torso forward while maintaining hip contact with the trapped shoulder. Never jerk or spike the shoulder rotation. Watch for your partner's tap signals continuously throughout the application, and release immediately upon any verbal or physical tap. In training, stop short of maximum extension, giving your partner time to assess their shoulder position and tap before the joint reaches its anatomical end range.

flashcards.question: How does the armbar-omoplata chain create a strategic dilemma for the defender?
flashcards.answer: The chain forces a binary decision where both options lead to a submission threat. If the defender keeps their arm straight to deny the omoplata angle, the armbar finish remains available with full extension leverage. If they bend the arm to defend the armbar, they create the shoulder angle needed for the omoplata transition. This dilemma compounds over time as the attacker switches between threats, progressively degrading the defender's ability to commit fully to either defense.

plausible: Bent arm is always the safer choice

flashcards.question: What grip adjustments are necessary as you transition from armbar position to omoplata position?
flashcards.answer: During the armbar phase, both hands control the opponent's wrist with thumbs on the inside. As you initiate the omoplata transition, your far hand releases the wrist to post on the mat for the sit-up while your near hand maintains unilateral wrist control. Once seated, both hands shift to control the opponent's far hip and belt line. This grip migration from wrist-wrist to wrist-post to hip-hip follows the changing control priorities from arm isolation to shoulder rotation finishing mechanics.
flashcards.answer_line: Wrist to post to hip control

plausible: Keep both hands on the wrist
trap: Release all grips to sit up

flashcards.question: What is the correct release protocol after your opponent taps to the omoplata?
flashcards.answer: Immediately stop all forward pressure and body rotation upon feeling or hearing the tap. Release your leg pinch around the trapped shoulder by opening your knees outward. Unwind your hip position to neutral, completely removing rotational force from the shoulder joint. Allow your opponent to slowly extract their arm at their own pace without pulling or manipulating the limb. Check for any signs of shoulder injury before resuming training, and give your partner adequate time to assess their mobility.

plausible: Pull the arm out for them

flashcards.question: How do you adjust if your leg gets caught on the opponent's head during the swing-over?
flashcards.answer: If your leg stalls halfway over their head, use your free hand to push off the mat and create additional hip elevation, giving your leg clearance to complete the arc. Simultaneously, use your posted foot to drive your hips upward and angle them toward the opponent's far side. If the leg remains stuck, grip the back of your own knee with your free hand and manually assist the leg over. Avoid forcing the leg through by kicking, as this risks injuring your partner's face or neck.

defender.name: Omoplata from Armbar Control Defender
defender.description: Defend against the omoplata from armbar control in BJJ. Recognition cues, escape timing, defensive options, and survival strategies for all skill levels.
defender.overview: Defending the omoplata from armbar control demands early recognition that the attacker is abandoning the armbar in favor of a shoulder lock. The transition period, when the attacker swings their leg over your head, represents the primary escape window. Once the omoplata is fully established with the attacker seated and controlling your far hip, defensive options narrow dramatically. Your priorities are preventing the leg from crossing over your shoulder, maintaining posture to avoid being flattened, and executing a forward roll before hip control is established if the omoplata begins to set. Understanding the attacker's sequence allows you to identify which phase of the attack you are in and select the appropriate defensive response for maximum escape probability.
key_principles: Recognize the transition early by feeling for the leg swing and hip rotation — every second of delay reduces your escape options significantly
Keep your trapped arm close to your body and avoid reaching away, which deepens the shoulder entanglement and accelerates the finish
Maintain an upright posture with your free hand posted on the mat to resist being flattened face-down by the attacker's forward pressure
The forward roll is your highest-percentage escape but only works before the attacker establishes far hip control — timing is everything
Never attempt to explosively muscle out of a locked omoplata, as this spikes rotational force on the shoulder and risks acute injury
If escape options have closed and the shoulder is loaded under pressure, tap early and decisively to protect long-term shoulder health
recognition_cues: Attacker's far leg begins lifting away from your body or swinging in an arc over your head from the armbar position
Attacker releases one hand from your wrist while maintaining single-hand control, indicating preparation for the transition
Attacker's hips begin rotating from the perpendicular armbar alignment toward a parallel seated position facing the same direction as you
Extension pressure on your elbow decreases and is replaced by a rotational loading sensation on your shoulder as the leg crosses over

defensive_options.action: Forward roll escape before hip control is established
defensive_options.when_to_use: Immediately upon recognizing the leg has crossed your shoulder and before the attacker sits up and grips your far hip
defensive_options.if_successful: You clear the omoplata entanglement entirely and land in the attacker's closed guard or recover to a neutral standing position
defensive_options.risk: If the attacker has already established hip control, the roll is blocked and you end up flattened with the omoplata tighter than before

defensive_options.action: Posture up and retract arm during the transition phase
defensive_options.when_to_use: During the leg swing when the attacker's legs are open and shoulder entanglement is not yet secured
defensive_options.if_successful: You extract your arm from the developing omoplata and return to defending the standard armbar, which may be easier to manage
defensive_options.risk: If you straighten the arm during retraction, you may expose yourself to the original armbar finish

defensive_options.action: Turn into attacker and stack to relieve shoulder pressure
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the omoplata is partially set but the attacker has not fully committed to the forward lean finish
defensive_options.if_successful: You compress the attacker's legs and create space to extract your shoulder, recovering to their guard or a scramble position
defensive_options.risk: Turning the wrong direction can deepen the shoulder rotation and accelerate the finish against you

escape_paths: Forward roll before hip control is established, using momentum to clear the shoulder entanglement and recover posture in the attacker's guard
Posture up and extract arm during the transition phase when the attacker is moving from armbar to omoplata and their leg control is loose
Turn into attacker and stack their legs to compress the omoplata structure and create space for shoulder extraction

favorable_outcomes.how: Execute the forward roll escape before the attacker establishes far hip control, using momentum to clear the omoplata entanglement and land in their closed guard where you can reset to a neutral passing situation

common_errors.error: Waiting too long to initiate escape and defending only after the omoplata is fully locked with hip control
common_errors.consequence: Escape options decrease dramatically once the attacker is seated with tight leg control and far hip grip, leaving only the tap as a realistic option
common_errors.correction: Begin escape immediately when you feel the leg swinging over your head, targeting the transition window before the attacker completes the sit-up and establishes hip control

common_errors.error: Attempting the forward roll without checking whether the attacker has established hip control first
common_errors.consequence: If the attacker has hip control, the forward roll is blocked and the rolling attempt flattens you face-down with the omoplata significantly tighter
common_errors.correction: Assess whether your far hip is free before committing to the roll. If hip control is established, switch to a posture-based defense or turn-in escape instead

common_errors.error: Pulling trapped arm back forcefully against a locked omoplata entanglement
common_errors.consequence: Can worsen shoulder position by deepening internal rotation, increases acute injury risk to the rotator cuff, and may re-expose the arm to armbar attack
common_errors.correction: Keep the arm close to your body and focus on postural escape movements rather than arm extraction. Address the body position first, and the arm will follow naturally

common_errors.error: Reaching with free arm behind you instead of posting for base
common_errors.consequence: Removes your only structural support against being flattened, accelerates the face-down position that makes the omoplata finish nearly guaranteed
common_errors.correction: Always post your free hand on the mat in front of you or to the side, maintaining an upright frame that resists the attacker's forward pressure and preserves your escape options

flashcards.question: How do you recognize that the attacker is transitioning from armbar to omoplata?
flashcards.answer: The key recognition cues are the attacker's far leg lifting away from your body and beginning to swing over your head, a shift in their hip angle from perpendicular armbar alignment to rotating parallel, and the release of one hand from your wrist while the other maintains control. You will also feel decreased extension pressure on your elbow replaced by a rotational loading sensation on your shoulder as their leg crosses over. Recognizing these cues early gives you the maximum escape window.
flashcards.answer_line: Leg lifts and swings over head

plausible: Opponent's hips lift off the mat
trap: Wait until they fully sit up

flashcards.question: When should you tap to the omoplata from armbar control to prevent injury?
flashcards.answer: Tap immediately when you feel your shoulder being forced into internal rotation beyond your comfortable range and you cannot execute any remaining escape option. If the attacker has seated position with hip control established and your shoulder is rotating despite your defensive efforts, the mechanical advantage has shifted irreversibly. Tap before you feel sharp pain or a popping sensation — the shoulder joint can suffer permanent damage quickly once the rotational threshold is exceeded. Never hesitate to tap early in training.

plausible: The instant your arm is trapped
Only once you're flat on your back
trap: Wait until you hear a pop

flashcards.question: What is the most effective defensive option during the transition phase?
flashcards.answer: The most effective defense during the transition is the forward roll, executed before the attacker establishes far hip control. As soon as you recognize the leg swinging over your head, tuck your chin, commit your weight forward, and roll over your trapped shoulder. The roll must be initiated before the attacker sits up and grips your hip — once hip control is established, the roll becomes blocked and your best escape window closes. Timing is the decisive factor in this defense.

plausible: Posture up and pull arm free

flashcards.question: What common defensive mistake most often leads to injury in this position?
flashcards.answer: The most dangerous mistake is attempting to explosively posture up or muscle out against a fully locked omoplata with hip control. When the attacker has tight leg control and your shoulder is already loaded under rotational pressure, a sudden forceful postural change can spike the rotational force on the shoulder joint, causing acute injury to the rotator cuff or labrum. Instead, focus on incremental positional improvements or accept the tap if escape options have genuinely closed.

trap: Rolling hard away from the attacker

flashcards.question: How should you position your free arm when defending the omoplata transition?
flashcards.answer: Your free arm should immediately post on the mat on the far side of your body, creating a structural frame that prevents you from being flattened face-down. This posted arm gives you the base needed to resist the attacker's forward pressure and maintains enough space to attempt a forward roll or turn into the attacker. Never reach backward toward the attacker with your free hand, as this removes your only structural support against the flattening pressure that makes the finish nearly inescapable.
flashcards.answer_line: Post arm out on far side

plausible: Grab your own knee for base

training_progressions.focus: Identifying transition cues and building defensive reflexes
training_progressions.description: Partner performs the armbar-to-omoplata transition at slow speed while you practice identifying the cues: leg lift, hip rotation, grip change. React by immediately bending your arm, posting your free hand, and preparing for escape. Repeat 15-20 times per side with zero resistance to build recognition speed.

training_progressions.focus: Developing the forward roll escape with proper timing
training_progressions.description: Partner completes the omoplata transition at moderate speed. Practice the forward roll escape during the critical window before hip control is established. Partner provides feedback on timing — too early, too late, or correct. Perform 10-15 repetitions per round with 30% resistance, focusing on the moment hip control would be established.

training_progressions.phase: Phase 3: Full Defense Under Progressive Resistance
training_progressions.focus: Integrating all defensive options against live attacks
training_progressions.description: Start from armbar control bottom against escalating resistance from 50% to 75%. Partner attacks with the full armbar-to-omoplata chain while you apply appropriate defenses — posture recovery, forward roll, turn-in escape — based on the phase of attack. Alternate between partners for 3-minute rounds, building decision-making under genuine submission pressure.
